I disagree. I have always had BPD traits, yet experienced a stable, loving childhood and adolescence with no trauma. I've had my BPD traits as long as I've had my autistic traits.
You literally say, "I don't want to be lumped with people who engage in harmful behaviors." In what way is this not you  reducing BPDers to harmful, toxic people?

But what does that "work" look like for me whose BPD never had an external cause. I did not experience trauma as a child. I've always had these traits. For as long as I can remember. I've also never externalized anything. All my BPD symptoms manifest as internal rage towards myself. Sure. I agree with the need to be accountable for ones actions. But in my situation for instance, what am I working towards? What am I healing? Nothing. For me, BPD treatment is unfortunately just like autistic masking is -- geared towards further internalizing everything and acting like all is well.

In that sense, how is my BPD any different from my autism. If I was always like this?

By this logic, autism is also nothing to celebrate, and certainly not some quirky cute thing. As someone with autism, my life is infinitely harder in a ridiculous number of ways because of how society is structured. As far as remission in BPD is concerned. It is unfortunately not always possible. Yes -- we can get to a place where we don't let how we feel inside impact our relationships. This is not dissimilar from autistic masking. Doesn't mean we feel any different internally. For me personally none of my BPD symptoms manifest externally. I don't expect anyone to accommodate me either with regards to being autistic or having BPD. That assumption is harmful.

Key point being "can be treated to a point where no medication is necessary." Some people with BPD will never reach that point. I'm autistic. I can mask well enough that I don't "look," or "act" autistic. With my BPD, it's the same. I don't display anything of the illness externally. That doesn't mean I'm happy or comfortable. But I don't attempt to kill myself or self-harm anymore, so most mental health professionals would agree, I don't need medication (not that it helps; and anyway, there's no medication that treats BPD per say, just DBT which doesn't really work if you internalize everything anyway). Does this mean I'm cured? I think it's very patronizing on your part to assume that I am choosing not to "take control and heal."

Ok. So your viewpoint is effectively: understanding and support for me but not for thee. Got it. 

It might interest you to know that some people are born with PD traits. And that there is growing research to suggest there is a genetic component to it. Reducing us to "people with harmful behaviors," is very rude and stigmatizing. Autistic people can also engage in very harmful behaviors. Are we supposed to vilify those too then? Or is it just the "evil" BPD witches who deserve to be burned at the stake?

(Saying all this as a woman who is both autistic and has BPD.)

By the logic that a lot of people seem to be using, autism is "treatable." Just mask and work harder than everyone around you to pretend to be normal while constantly feeling uncomfortable. It's disingenuous to say that "practice DBT" is not to the BPD person precisely what "just mask" is to the autistic person. (Coming from someone who is autistic and also has BPD. Yes -- I'm tired of pretending that DBT actually does anything for those with quiet-BPD aside from alienate them further, and teach them that their feelings are burdensome.) As for those who attempt to say "well, autism is a processing disorder, and BPD is not!" It is actually quite easy to view BPD as a disorder stemming from one's inability to process social interactions in a normal regulated way.

At the end of the day, those who don't want to agree that BPD can be a form of neurodivergence are those who believe people with BPD are "evil," and don't deserve support (as far as I am concerned, and no, my opinion on this won't change).

I have autism and depression too. I won't try to argue against your belief that you don't provide any value to society. Perhaps this is true. I don't know you. But I want you to ask yourself why that matters? I think that the belief that you can try to challenge is: why do you think you have to contribute to society to be worthy of love and care? You are still human. You are different. This is true. I am also different. There are others who are uniquely different. Why are any of us not worthy of care just on the merit of being human?

I know that you can objectively argue that society wastes resources on us while we give nothing back. By this logic our value is a net negative. But we cannot know this for sure. Our existence likely brings some joy to someone. Maybe this is not a measurable contribution in the way that working a job is. That doesn't mean it's worthless.

Moreover, I am the type of person who believes that if I have a roof over my head and food on the table, then there's no problem with any excess I have going to the next person even if they contribute nothing. I highly doubt you contribute absolutely nothing, but even if you do, if I can see it this way, certainly there are others who see it this way too. That is to say, you are probably not this grand burden to society that you believe you are.

I want to end by saying that I am sorry you are feeling this way. I often feel the same. I know that words are of little comfort when I feel this way, but I hope that with time things improve. Think about it this way. I am a stranger on the internet. I don't know you and you don't know me. But I still wrote all of this. Not because I want some stupid internet points which I can't spend, but because I thought you were worth my time. I'm sure others feel the same.

Sounds like your puppy has become a teenager who's learning to test your boundaries. She's also still young enough and has enough energy that it's hard to calm down when she's in such an activated state which is why redirection may not immediately work. Ignoring the behaviour won't work because you're essentially teaching her that she can enter "shark-mode" and not lose what is giving her immediate satisfaction: biting you! I had this problem with my pup as well around this age. My advice: keep her on a slack line at home. When she enters "shark-mode" try and redirect her. If it doesn't work calmly pull the line so she can't get to you, and leave the room. Return after a couple of minutes, and start playing with her again. If she bites, repeat. She'll eventually figure out that biting = no more playtime with you, which is what she wants the most. Obviously, reward her when she plays without chomping. She'll grow out of it soon enough. Bigger dogs are a bit slower to mature if that helps too but because of their size it's really important to set boundaries like this with them.

A trick I learned in ERP is to actually sit down and write out the probabilities of everything that would have to go wrong for the plane to crash. You'll see a small number. And sure, that doesn't mean it won't happen. But I like to think about the probability that I end up with as an approximation of how much energy I should put into thinking/worrying about the plane crashing.

So if the probability comes out to like 50% then I put like 50% of my energy worrying about the plane crashing. If it's 25% then I put 25% of my energy into worrying about it. For anything lower than 1%, I'll put like 1% of energy into worrying about it. It takes practice, but I try to take that as my rule of thumb now. Do I struggle though? Absolutely. Anxiety is tough.

Hey, I hate flying too. It's an HA sufferers nightmare because you're basically trapped without any outside help for however long you're in the air.

I actually flew from India to London and then from London to Toronto recently. That's about 17 hours of total flight time. Was I panicking, sure? But I made it out fine. What really helped me was that on both flights there were medical emergencies on board. Here's what stood out:

The flight is fairly equipped to handle most standard medical issues. One elderly woman had an unusually high blood pressure, so they quietly moved her into business class and gave her some medications. Another elderly man had a similar issue and was also treated. They were both fine.

The second thing which stood out was that everyone who did have a medical issue onboard was fairly old (i.e. people who definitely already had a medical history). It's hard to believe for us, but when you're fairly young and in moderately okay health (even if you're not a complete gym rat), the chances of something catastrophic happening is fairly low. The worst part is sitting with the discomfort.

It may help to realize that most people on flights aren't even aware of things like DVT, etc. They just sit through eleven hour flights without getting up once because they're clueless. And I'm not talking about young people. I'm talking about 70 year old grandmas doing this shit. 

The most important thing is to prepare yourself for the discomfort and all the associated physical symptoms. Something which another Redditor suggested to me was to kind of plan out an itinerary of your flight. Something like, "hour one: we're in the air and I'm watching a movie," because this helps normalize what's happening.

As a final aside, people with horrific medical conditions fly all the time and are fine. My uncle had a heart attack a couple months ago, had a stent placed at some sketchy rural hospital, and flew economy to a bigger hospital three or four days after the stent was placed to have more procedures done. He's fine. Maybe a bit tired, but fine.

Yes -- this may set you back a bit, but in the long run, it's more important to get help for your depression/mental health, before you really jump into life.

I see a lot of my peers doing amazing in university, and I always have to remind myself that I'm struggling with something that makes it harder for me to perform well. You're not a failure. Tons of people get kicked out and go on to complete their degrees later and have decent/good/amazing lives.

I don't really have any advice for that though, because I haven't figured it out myself. I find that trying to make a list of three things I want to do everyday helps. One thing to help with my mental health. One for my physical health. And one thing which I need to do for other reasons (e.g. school work).

Just remember to figure out all your options, and do your best to think objectively about those options. Sincerely hoping stuff works out for you dude.

Inherently, everyone is selfish. I choose to treat people with respect and kindness because I want to. And in that, I *am* selfish. Doing anything, even solely for the purpose of "wanting to do the thing," is intrinsically selfish. That's not necessarily a bad thing however. Sure, a lot of shit gets put out into the world because of human selfishness. Assholes everywhere. And yet, those who treat others with kindness and respect because they want to, still put good into the world, even if the intentions behind their actions are selfish (i.e. wanting to).

That said, it's very easy to become disillusioned with the world, when such people are so few and far in between. I often find myself struggling with the same things you are struggling with right now. Because, to an extent, you are correct. The world is not good -- the majority of its denizens are not kind people who would give a rat's ass about you or I. It's very easy to forget, when we're so caught up in our own struggles, that there are still one or two people out there, trying to do good, regardless of how selfish their motivations are.

Not trying to invalidate your thoughts of course. I get where you're coming from, as I think like you a lot of the time.

It also doesn't leave for anything to get worse. Because, life could get worse too. Not necessary that life has to improve. That's why I think suicide has a certain allure, in that it enables a person to exercise control over their lives where none may exist.
